name: check an answer by the letters it has to contain
one_line: The letters of the question are printed in alphabetical order, and an answer whose letters do not match them is wrong whatever it says.
how: Take a short phrase — IL MARE CALMO, eleven letters — and print its letters once, in alphabetical order, on a line of their own: a a c e i l l m m o r. Under it print the word lengths of the answer in brackets, 5 2 4, and blanks to match. Say how to check: sort the letters of whatever was written and compare them one at a time with the printed line; if they differ the answer is wrong however well it reads. It rejects and never confirms, and the sheet should say so. The lengths are not decoration — without them the 1 024 ways of putting spaces into eleven letters are all open, and with them one is. Sort both sides yourself first.

knobs.knob: whether the sorted letters are printed
knobs.effect: Printed, the person throws out their own wrong answers and the sheet needs no solution page. Not printed, nothing on the page can reject anything and the only test left is whether it sounds right.

knobs.knob: whether the word lengths are given
knobs.effect: Given, one division into words survives out of 1 024. Withheld, all of them stay open, and the work stops being about letters and becomes about where the spaces go.
Four all different is 24 orderings and the whole list prints on four lines. Five is 120 and eight is 40 320, so past four the list goes and the sorted line is all the sheet has left.

Repeats let the count be worked out instead of listed: MAMMA is 120 over six over two, which is ten, and writing eleven rows means two are the same. Little else in this chapter checks itself that cleanly.

where_the_work_is: In the phrase, which has to be an anagram of another phrase and has to be found before anything is printed. Sorting the letters afterwards is mechanical; finding the pair is not.
breaks: The sorted line is the whole error check, so it must not run over a line end — set it in one row or it stops working. Scanned back, a hand-sorted string of letters is the hardest thing on the page to read. On 800x480 eleven letters and three numbers fit and the blanks do not. Composing needs a hand: the pair has to be found and both sides sorted and compared before anything goes to the printer.
